design_detail: Online randomized between-participants experiment with a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design (the authors call it a cross-sectional online study with a randomised design). UK adults from the Prolific research panel (June 2022) each read one of eight simulated BBC-branded news stories about a death reported at an inquest, adapted from a real BBC online report about an ecstasy death in 2019, varying the decedent's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 years, had used the drug 'once or twice'; or 43 years, had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy/MDMA or heroin), each with a matching face photograph from the Chicago Face Database. Primary outcome: a bespoke 9-item measure of stigma towards the depicted person; second outcome: a 6-item measure of support for harm-reduction policies; both answered once, straight after the story and attention checks. Primary analysis: 2 × 2 × 2 MANOVA on the two outcomes; exploratory four-step hierarchical regressions on participant characteristics (demographics, political orientation and conservatism, belief in a just world, empathic perspective-taking, drug knowledge, general stigma, familiarity, having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death). Not pre-registered. Ethics approval from Liverpool John Moores University (22/PHI/010).
can_establish: That among UK adults on an online panel reading one simulated news report of a drug-related death, a male, an older (43, 15 years of regular use) and a heroin decedent drew higher self-reported stigma towards the person depicted than a female, a younger (21, first-time) and an ecstasy decedent (by the editors' calculation about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations), and that the older version drew slightly higher stated support for harm-reduction policies (about 0.1 standard deviation), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories and not in the heroin stories.
cannot_establish: Whether these differences last beyond the survey or change behaviour, votes or policy (one short story read once, a new outcome measure answered immediately); whether age itself or the use history attached to it (first-time against 15 years of regular use) produced the age effects (they were manipulated together); how real news, with its own photographs and framing, works; or that participant traits in the exploratory regressions (just-world belief, empathy, politics) cause stigma (observational, with about 30% of participants missing from those models by the editors' calculation).

sample.recruitment: Online research panel (Prolific, UK) in June 2022: members were invited by email with a one-line topic description (how people respond to drug-related news stories), the time needed and the payment (a small monetary reward managed by the panel), and gave consent on a Qualtrics survey (p. 3, Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Living in the UK and aged over 18, from panel profiles checked by screening questions (p. 3). 1280 recruited; 32 clicked the link but did not proceed, leaving 1248 (97.5%). Completing the survey in under 5 minutes (half the pilot median of 10) would have led to exclusion, and none did; attention checks on the story's gender, age and drug withdrew no one (p. 5, Procedure).
sample.demographics: Mean age 45.7 (SD 15.4); 51.0% women; 57.4% with a degree or above; 86.7% White/White British; median household income band £25,000–49,900; voting preference left 62.6%, centre 13.3%, right 24.2%; lifetime use of any drug 53.5%, cannabis 51.0%, MDMA/ecstasy 16.6%, heroin/methadone 3.8%; 79.2% had seen a drug-related death in the media and 52.2% harm reduction in the media (Table 1, p. 6).
sample.attrition: 32 of 1280 (2.5%) did not proceed past the link; whether this was before randomization is not stated. The degrees of freedom imply 1238 participants in the MANOVA (F1,1230 and F2,1229), 1240 in the one-way test in Table 1 (F7,1232) and 868 in the regressions (F17,850 and F16,851) (editors' calculation); none of these exclusions is reported. Familiarity answers of 'none of the above' and general-stigma answers of 'prefer not to say' were recoded as missing (pp. 4–5).
sample.selection_effects: A commercial online panel of people who chose to take part for payment; matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only, with degree holders (57% against 42% in the UK) and people preferring left-wing parties (63% against 39% at the 2019 general election) over-represented (p. 9). Findings apply at most to UK adults on such panels.

exposure.measurement: Random allocation to one of eight story versions. The changed text was the name and pronouns (Jane or John), the stated age and use history (21 and 'once or twice', or 43 and regularly for 15 years) and the drug (ecstasy, MDMA in the coroner's sentence, or heroin); the image showed a White person with a neutral expression, described as matched on rated age (21 or 24 years) and attractiveness; Flesch Reading Ease 63 for all stories; piloted with departmental colleagues (pp. 3–4; Fig. 1). In the published example (young, ecstasy) the brother who speaks at the inquest is 26; in the template's older version he is 48. Comprehension checks on the story's gender, age and drug followed the story.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: a single written news story, read once.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable to the stimulus (one drug named per story). Participants' own drug use was recorded (Table 1) and not used in the analyses.

comparison.controls: Factorial contrasts within the experiment: female against male decedent, younger against older, ecstasy against heroin; there is no story-free or neutral comparison condition.
comparison.matching: Randomization. The authors state that measured covariates were balanced across groups (Table 1) without reporting tests; editors' check: women made up 44.9% to 62.6% of the eight groups, chi-square 11.5, df 7, p about 0.12, compatible with chance.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparison. Empathy and just-world beliefs may have been measured before the story (Limitations) or after it (Procedure); see reporting issues.

outcomes.instruments: Stigma towards the depicted person (primary): a bespoke nine-item measure with blame, anger and pity items adapted from the Attribution Questionnaire (AQ-9), one controllability and one responsibility item, and four social-distance items after McGinty et al.; each 1–9, total 9–81, higher meaning more stigma; Cronbach's α=.81 (pp. 3–4). Support for harm reduction: a culturally adapted version of the measure of Wild et al. (2021), six items (general harm-reduction programmes, government funding for harm reduction, drug checking services, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone, opioid agonist therapies), each 1–5, totalled; α=.88 (p. 4). Covariates: political conservatism (four items, α=.78), the empathic perspective-taking scale of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (α=.75), the Global Belief in a Just World Scale (seven items, α=.88), a Level of Familiarity scale (11 items, α=0.74), general stigma towards people with substance use problems (four items, α=.80), self-rated drug knowledge, own drug use, and having seen media coverage of harm reduction and of families affected by a drug-related death (pp. 4–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The stigma measure is new; only internal consistency is reported. Item-level results are in Supplementary S2, not read.
outcomes.operationalization: Stigma is the total of the nine items; the pity item and the social-distance items are worded so that a higher answer means less stigma, and their reverse-scoring is not described. Support for harm reduction is the total of six policy ratings given after general descriptions of each approach, presented separately from the story. A criminal-justice diversion item was collected for a separate analysis and excluded (p. 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: alpha .05 for all tests (p. 5). The MANOVA tests the two outcomes jointly; the univariate follow-ups, the interaction probe and two four-step regressions with up to 17 predictors are uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-reported outcomes. Participants saw only their own story and were told the study was about responses to drug-related news stories (p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD) and univariate F(1,1230) (p. 5): stigma, male against female decedent 45.6 (12.1) against 43.4 (12.6), F=11.1, p<.001; older against younger 46.7 (11.8) against 42.3 (12.7), F=40.5, p<.001; heroin against ecstasy 46.9 (11.5) against 42.1 (12.8), F=50.1, p<.001. Harm-reduction support: age F=4.5, p=.035 (printed 22.98 against 23.57, the first being the younger group by the editors' check against Table 1); gender F=.0, p=.802; drug F=.0, p=.922; age × drug interaction F(2,1229)=4.9, p=.007, ecstasy stories older against younger F=4.8, p=.029 (printed 22.7 against 23.89, younger first). Editors' calculations (standardized mean differences with pooled SD, approximate 95% intervals using the Table 1 group sizes): stigma heroin against ecstasy d≈0.39 (0.28 to 0.51), older against younger d≈0.36 (0.25 to 0.47), male against female d≈0.18 (0.07 to 0.29); harm-reduction support older against younger d≈0.12 (0.01 to 0.23), ecstasy stories older against younger d≈0.24 (0.08 to 0.39); partial eta squared from the F values 0.009 (gender), 0.032 (age) and 0.039 (drug) for stigma and 0.004 (age) for harm-reduction support. Exploratory regressions: stigma final R²=.569 (F17,850=65.9); harm-reduction support final R²=.379 (F printed as 3247; about 32.5 by the editors' recalculation from R²) (p. 7).
analysis.covariates: None in the MANOVA (covariates judged balanced). The regressions entered the story factors, then age, sex, education and household income, then political orientation, political conservatism, belief in a just world and empathic perspective-taking, then support for harm reduction (stigma model only), drug knowledge, general stigma, familiarity and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death (p. 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the protocol was not pre-registered and that the findings should be considered exploratory (p. 9).
analysis.selective_reporting: Item-level analyses are only in Supplementary S2 (not read), yet the Discussion draws on them (older decedents rated more responsible and in control, with more blame and anger; p. 8). Hypotheses were stated in advance in the paper, but without registration the choice of total scores, the MANOVA and the regression steps cannot be checked against a plan; a diversion-programme item was collected for another analysis.
analysis.power: A priori calculation for a medium effect (f=0.25, power 0.95) gave a minimum of 54 (p. 3); with 1248 the study could detect effects far smaller than those found.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In UK online-panel adults, one simulated news story about a drug-related death produced small to moderate differences in self-reported stigma towards the depicted person by the decedent's gender, age with use history and drug (about 0.2 to 0.4 standard deviations; 1% to 4% of variance), and a very small difference in stated support for harm-reduction policies by age with use history (about 0.1 standard deviation), confined to the ecstasy stories; the drug and the decedent's gender did not change support for harm reduction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the sample a "nationally representative sample (UK)" (p. 1), while it was matched on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented degree holders and left-wing voters (p. 9). The abstract and conclusions describe associations, appropriately cautious for an exploratory experiment, but the conclusions then advise campaigners and media producers on framing and images (p. 10) from one exposure measured immediately. The discussion suggests that reporting more opioid deaths, to match the mortality profile, may lead to higher stigma (p. 8), an extrapolation from one heroin story. It reports greater support after older than younger heroin deaths (p. 9), contradicting the results, the abstract and the next sentence of the discussion (ecstasy) and Table 1 (no age difference among the heroin stories); and it lists having seen media accounts of a family affected by a drug-related death among predictors of higher support (p. 9), while Table 3 and the results show that predictor was not significant. The age manipulation also changed the use history (once or twice against 15 years of regular use), the brother's age, and possibly the photograph's apparent age, so 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'; the authors note the use-history explanation themselves (p. 9).

timeline.event: Forsyth's quantitative study of drug-fatality reports in the popular press, cited here as showing that UK press reports over-represented young women and ecstasy deaths; not read.
Kelly & Westerhoff randomized clinicians to two terms for a person with a substance-related condition (on the project's language-and-stigma list; not read for this card).
Forsyth: of 18 alleged mephedrone deaths named in online news, the most linked were later reported not to involve the drug causally (card sc_forsyth_2012).
Pennington et al.: registered-report vignette experiment on labels and models of problematic substance use and stigma, about a living person (card sc_pennington_2023).
This study: first experiment, by the authors' account, on how news depictions of a drug-related death affect public stigma and support for harm reduction.

replication.where_it_stands: The authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug-related deaths. Related vignette experiments concern labels for living people (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010; Pennington et al., 2023). The findings are exploratory (not pre-registered) and await a pre-registered replication with real news items, separate manipulation of age and use history, delayed outcomes and a behavioural measure.

funding.funder: Not reported: the paper has ethics and interest declarations but no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work (p. 10, Declarations of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Public Health Institute and School of Psychology, Liverpool John Moores University; School of Psychological Sciences, University of Bristol; Faculty of Health Sciences and Sport, University of Stirling (p. 1). The lead author's earlier experiments on messaging about drug consumption rooms and on representations of people who use drugs are cited in support; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered randomized experiment in a probability sample, using real published news reports varied one feature at a time (decedent gender, age apart from use history, drug, ethnicity, framing and images), with a validated stigma measure, a behavioural or policy-choice outcome, and follow-up after days or weeks.

domains.note: Automated online allocation to eight conditions, concealed by design; group differences in Table 1 look like chance (sex across groups: chi-square 11.5, df 7, p about 0.12, editors' calculation) plus typographical errors.
Everyone read the allocated story; all passed the comprehension checks; analysed as allocated.

For the main analysis about 10 of 1248 (0.8%) are missing by the degrees of freedom, unexplained but too few to matter. The exploratory regressions lost about 30% (868 analysed), which concerns those analyses only.

Self-reported attitudes answered immediately after the story by participants who knew the topic; a new stigma measure with internal consistency only and undescribed reverse-scoring; demand effects possible, though each participant saw one condition.
Not pre-registered; two outcomes analysed jointly, item-level results in a supplement, an extra item collected for another paper; the authors call the findings exploratory.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large randomized experiment with little missing data for the main analysis and an open statement that it is exploratory. Concerns are the absence of registration, a new outcome measure without validity data, outcomes measured once straight after one simulated story, the bundling of age with use history, and several reporting errors (Table 1 cells, a regression F, harm-reduction means printed in reverse order, discussion statements that contradict the results). It may be cited, as an experiment, for the direction and approximate size of differences in self-reported stigma towards a depicted decedent by gender, age with use history and drug, and for the very small differences in stated support for harm-reduction policies, in UK adults on an online panel. It may not be cited for effects on real behaviour, on policy or over time, for the effect of age apart from use history, or for participant traits causing stigma.

key_findings.finding: UK adults (n=1280) were recruited from the Prolific panel in June 2022 and randomized to one of eight simulated news stories; thirty-two clicked the survey link but did not proceed, leaving 1248 (97.5%). Eligibility: living in the UK, aged over 18; the sample was matched to the UK adult population on sex, age and ethnicity. An a priori calculation for a medium effect (f=0.25, power 0.95) gave a minimum of 54.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Design; Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The stories were adapted from a BBC online report of an ecstasy death in 2019, kept its branding and length, and varied the decedent's gender (Jane or John), age with use history (21 years and 'once or twice', or 43 years and regular use for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin), with a White, neutral-expression face from the Chicago Face Database matched on rated age (21 or 24 years) and attractiveness; Flesch Reading Ease 63; piloted with departmental colleagues.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Materials › Stimuli, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 3); Fig. 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: In the Fig. 1 example (Jane, young, ecstasy; read on the rendered page, the figure being an image) the brother at the inquest is 26; in the printed template (older version, p. 3) he is 48, a change not marked as manipulated text.

key_findings.finding: Outcomes: stigma towards the depicted person on a bespoke nine-item measure (blame, anger and pity adapted from the AQ-9; controllability; responsibility; four social-distance items), each 1–9, total 9–81, higher meaning more stigma, α=.81; support for six harm-reduction policies (general programmes, government funding, drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone, opioid agonist therapy) on an adapted version of the measure of Wild et al. (2021), each 1–5, totalled, α=.88.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4) and 2nd paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Procedure: demographic questions, then randomization to a story, comprehension checks on the story's gender, age and drug (no one withdrawn), the primary outcome, then the remaining questions; a completion time under 5 minutes (half the 10-minute pilot median) was the exclusion rule and excluded no one. Ethics approval: Liverpool John Moores University Research Ethics Committee, reference 22/PHI/010.

MANOVA on stigma and harm-reduction support: main effects of gender (Wilks' Λ=.99; F2,1229=9.1, p<.001), age (Λ=.93; F=45.2, p<.001) and drug (Λ=.94; F=36.9, p<.001); gender × age (F=.1, p=.869) and gender × drug (F=2.3, p=.099) not significant; age × drug significant (Λ=.99; F=4.9, p=.007); gender × age × drug not significant (F=.1, p=.926).

Stigma towards the depicted person was higher for male than female decedents (mean 45.6, SD 12.1, against 43.4, SD 12.6; F1,1230=11.1, p<.001), for older than younger decedents (46.7, SD 11.8, against 42.3, SD 12.7; F=40.5, p<.001) and for heroin than ecstasy deaths (46.9, SD 11.5, against 42.1, SD 12.8; F=50.1, p<.001).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: d≈0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; partial eta squared 0.009, 0.032 and 0.039.

key_findings.finding: Support for harm reduction was higher after older than younger decedents (F1,1230=4.5, p=.035; printed as 22.98, SD 5.09, against 23.57, SD 4.78); there was no main effect of gender (F=.0, p=.802) or drug (F=.0, p=.922); in the ecstasy stories support was higher after the older than the younger decedent (F1,1230=4.8, p=.029; printed as 22.7, SD 5.4, against 23.89, SD 4.67).
key_findings.note: The means are printed younger first although the sentence names the older group first: weighting the Table 1 cell means by group size gives older 23.6 against younger 23.0, older ecstasy 23.9 against younger ecstasy 22.7, and older heroin 23.3 against younger heroin 23.3 (editors' calculation). Editors' d≈0.12 (age) and 0.24 (ecstasy stories).

key_findings.finding: By condition, mean stigma ranged from 38.6 (Jane, young, ecstasy) to 50.1 (John, old, heroin) (F7,1232=14.67, p<0.001) and harm-reduction support from 22.4 to 24.0. Whole sample: mean age 45.7 (SD 15.4), 51.0% women, 57.4% with a degree, 86.7% White/White British; lifetime use of any drug 53.5%, cannabis 51.0%, MDMA/ecstasy 16.6%, heroin/methadone 3.8%; 79.2% had seen a drug-related death in the media.

Exploratory regression for stigma, final step (R²=.569; F17,850=65.9, p<.001): male (B=1.959), older (B=4.826) and heroin (B=4.665) decedents, stronger belief in a just world (B=.222), lower empathic perspective-taking (B=-.227), lower support for harm reduction (B=-.717) and higher general stigma towards people with substance use problems (B=1.347) went with higher stigma, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death with lower stigma (B=-1.518, p<.05); political orientation, conservatism, drug knowledge and familiarity were not significant. The story factors alone gave R²=.068; the later steps added .016, .234 and .251.

Exploratory regression for harm-reduction support, final step (R²=.379): older decedent (B=.675, p<.05), empathic perspective-taking (B=.095), drug knowledge (B=.178) and familiarity (B=.135) went with more support; older participant age (B=-.018), right-wing against left-wing orientation (B=-1.486), political conservatism (B=-.485) and general stigma (B=-.389) with less; having seen coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death was not significant (B=-.192, SE .344). The story factors alone gave R²=.007.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results, 6th paragraph (p. 7, continuing on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the protocol was not pre-registered, so the findings should be considered exploratory; empathic perspective-taking and just-world beliefs were presented before the stimuli and may have primed responses; photographs came from a face database rather than the kinds used in news; a single written story may not reflect how people now consume news; decedent ethnicity was not varied. Degree holders (57% against 42% in the UK population) and people preferring left-wing parties (63% against 39% at the 2019 general election) were over-represented but balanced across groups.

The authors suggest that rebalancing news reports towards the commoner opioid deaths may raise stigma towards decedents; report from item-level analyses (Supplementary S2) that older decedents were rated more responsible for, and more in control of, their deaths and drew more blame and anger; and suggest that the longer use attached to the older decedent may explain the greater support for harm reduction.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 8) and 5th paragraph (p. 8, continuing on p. 9)
key_findings.note: The item-level analyses are in a supplement not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The harm-reduction means are printed in the reverse order of the comparison named: 'older compared to younger' is followed by 22.98 against 23.57, and 'older ecstasy decedent compared to younger' by 22.7 against 23.89; the group-size-weighted Table 1 means show the first number is the younger group in both (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction stated in words (older higher) is right; anyone reading the numbers in printed order would reverse it.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says support was greater after older than younger heroin deaths, while the results, the abstract and the following sentence of the discussion place the age difference in the ecstasy stories, and Table 1 shows no age difference among the heroin stories (23.3 against 23.3, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The heroin statement is an error; cite the ecstasy interaction.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion lists having seen media accounts of a family affected by a drug-related death among predictors of higher harm-reduction support, while Table 3 (B=-.192, SE .344, not significant) and the results say it was not a significant predictor.
reporting_issues.consequence: That statement in the discussion is unsupported by the paper's own analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The harm-reduction regression is reported as F16,851 = 3247; with R²=.379, 16 predictors and 851 residual degrees of freedom, F is about 32.5 (editors' calculation; the stigma model's F of 65.9 recomputes correctly).

Missing data are not reported: the MANOVA degrees of freedom imply 1238 participants analysed, the one-way test in Table 1 1240, and both regressions 868 (69.6% of 1248), against 1248 reported (editors' calculations).
reporting_issues.consequence: The main analysis is barely affected; the exploratory regressions rest on a subsample whose difference from the full sample is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 cells are internally inconsistent: White/White British is 56.5% in condition 2 (82.6% to 88.5% elsewhere), but the overall 86.7% is reproduced only if that cell is about 86.5%; lifetime cannabis use (59.7%) exceeds lifetime use of any drug (52.3%) in condition 3; and the centre (23.5%) and right-wing (10.9%) percentages of condition 8 reproduce the overall 13.3% and 24.2% only if swapped (editors' calculations).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors in the balance table; the statement that covariates were balanced was not tested in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The order of measures is described inconsistently: the Procedure puts demographics before randomization and the remaining questions after the outcome, while the Limitations say empathic perspective-taking and just-world beliefs were presented before the stimuli.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether these covariates could have been changed by the story (if measured after) or could have primed the responses (if before).

reporting_issues.issue: Participant sex has the same coding label as the story factor (male vs female), yet in step 3 of Table 2 its coefficient is positive (B=1.603) while the text says being female predicted higher stigma, and in Table 3 it is negative (B=-.967) while the text says being male predicted higher support.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the participant-sex effects cannot be determined from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The stigma total runs 9–81 with higher scores meaning more stigma, but the pity item and the four social-distance items are worded so that a higher answer means less stigma; reverse-scoring is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The scoring cannot be checked from the paper, presumably reversed.

reporting_issues.issue: The age manipulation changed more than age: the use history (once or twice against 15 years of regular use), the brother's age (26 in the young example, 48 in the older template), and the photographs, described as matched on rated ages of 21 or 24 years, which does not fit a decedent of 43.
reporting_issues.consequence: The age effects cannot be attributed to age alone; what the older photographs showed is unclear.

Supplementary materials S1 (stimuli) and S2 (item-level analyses), online with the article (doi:10.1016/j.drugpo.2022.103909), are not among the senior author's files and were not read.
